newsitem.title: CHINA: China rejects dissident's labour camp lawsuit.
newsitem.headline: China rejects dissident's labour camp lawsuit.

text.p: A Chinese court has rejected a lawsuit by veteran dissident Liu Xiaobo filed against Beijing authorities for sending him to a labour camp without trial, a human rights group said on Saturday.

In a decision issued on Friday, Beijing's Xuanwu District Court upheld a decision by the Beijing Re-education through Labour Committee to send Liu, 41, to a labour camp for three years, the Information Centre of Human Rights & Democratic Movement in China quoted Liu's wife, Liu Xia, as saying.

"A judge from the presiding office of the Xuanwu District Court notified Liu Xia that the court had already decided to reject the proposal made by Liu Xiaobo," the Hong Kong-based group said in a faxed statement.
Members of Liu's family could not immediately be reached for comment.

Police detained Liu Xiaobo, a prominent literary critic and democracy activist, last September and sent him to a camp in the northeastern city of Dalian for three years of re-education through labour.

Liu's lawsuit was heard on March 5 at the Dalian camp where he has been put to work making toothpicks, and was attended by Liu, his wife and parents, and a Beijing judge, the statement said. The decision was handed down on Friday.

The rejection of the suit comes on the heels of visits by U.S. Vice President Al Gore and Speaker of the U.S. House of Representatives Newt Gingrich, both of whom raised human rights and political freedoms -- long thorns in the side of bilateral ties -- with their hosts.
Beijing, eager to ensure nothing mars the growing Sino-U.S. rapprochement, stepped up surveillance of the families of jailed dissidents ahead of the visits, activists' relatives said.
Western human rights activists say re-education through labour is increasingly favoured as a way of removing dissidents from the public eye without the complications of a trial.
Liu's father Liu Lin had told the group his son was in good health and was not being worked too hard, the statement said.
"Moreover, the re-education through labour camp is not very far from his parents' residence, making it convenient for them to look after him," it said.

The Re-education through Labour Committee accused Liu Xiaobo of sullying the government and disturbing the social order for his part in a petition to the government and an article written for a Taiwan newspaper.
In the 1995 petition, Liu and dozens of other intellectuals urged Beijing to reassess the June 1989 military crackdown on student-led demonstrations in Tiananmen Square.
In the months before his detention, Liu orchestrated several daring, open letters to the government and called for the impeachment of Communist Party chief Jiang Zemin.
The U.S. State Department blasted Beijing in its annual report on human rights for effectively silencing public dissent in 1996 through jailings, intimidation, or exile.
